newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Militia leader trial opens at Rwanda tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Militia leader trial opens at Rwanda tribunal.

text.p: A U.N. tribunal on Rwanda's genocide opened its second trial on Tuesday with former Hutu militia leader Georges Rutaganda charged with genocide and crimes against humanity.
At the second full trial in this northern Tanzanian town, Rutaganda, 39, told the court before the prosecution and defence outlined their cases that Tuesday was his 13th wedding anniversary.
Prosecutor James Stewart said the prosecution would call 35 witnesses including civilians who survived the 1994 genocide and would prove there was a genocide and Rutaganda took part in it.
Rutaganda, a Hutu, was vice-president of the Interahamwe militia held responsible for massacres during the mass slaughter of an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically-moderate Hutus.
Under the rules of the U.N.'s Rwanda tribunal, Rutaganda faces life imprisonment if found guilty. His defence comprises Luc De Temmerman of Belgium and Canadian Tiphaine Dickson.

De Temmerman questioned whether a genocide ever took place in Rwanda in 1994 or whether the deprived Hutu majority sought equal rights with the Tutsi minority. He said he would call witnesses to describe whether there was a genocidal plan or not.
"We must examine the role of the Interahamwe and examine whether the massacres were planned or not," De Temmerman said.
Rutaganda has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The defence said he was a simple businessman and his position as a vice-president of the Interahamwe was only an official post and nothing more.

De Temmerman said the defence's witnesses would testify that the Tutsi-dominated rebel Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF) organised massacres after the April 6, 1994, killing of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana.
Rutaganda has been held in Arusha, where the tribunal has its headquarters, since his extradition from Zambia last May.

Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, was charged last May with eight counts of genocide, crimes against humanity (extermination), crimes against humanity (murder) and violations of Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions.

The trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu which began on January 9 was suspended until May 12 to give time for the defence to prepare after the prosecution completed its case. The tribunal has so far indicted 21 people.
